name: Dalbavancin / Oritavancin / Telavancin
evidenceNote: All three are FDA-approved for serious skin infections on the strength of large randomized phase 3 trials against vancomycin. Telavancin is also approved for certain hospital pneumonias.
summary: Dalbavancin, oritavancin and telavancin are FDA-approved IV antibiotics for serious skin infections, including MRSA. Two need only one dose.
keyTakeaway: Dalbavancin, oritavancin and telavancin are lipoglycopeptides: hospital antibiotics built on the same peptide core as vancomycin, with a fatty tail added. All three are FDA-approved by intravenous infusion for serious bacterial skin infections caused by Gram-positive germs such as MRSA. Dalbavancin and oritavancin last so long in the body that a single infusion can replace a week or two of daily drips; in phase 3 trials they matched vancomycin, with about 80 percent of patients responding early on either. Telavancin is given daily and carries a boxed warning about kidney harm and fetal risk.

blocks.text: Dalbavancin, oritavancin and telavancin are three related antibiotics grouped as lipoglycopeptides. Each is semisynthetic, meaning chemists start from a natural glycopeptide (a ring of amino acids decorated with sugars, the same family as vancomycin) and attach a lipid, or fatty, side chain [1][3][5]. That tail helps the drug cling to bacteria and, for two of the three, keeps it in the bloodstream for days.

They work only against Gram-positive bacteria, the group that includes Staphylococcus aureus and its drug-resistant form MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus), as well as streptococci. They are given only as an infusion into a vein, by a clinician, and are not available as pills [1][3][5].

rows: Skin infections; hospital and ventilator pneumonia [5]

sections.heading: How does this drug class work?

blocks.text: Bacteria wrap themselves in a cell wall made of peptidoglycan, a mesh of sugar chains tied together by short peptides. Dalbavancin grabs the end of those peptide links, a pair of amino acids called D-alanyl-D-alanine, so the links cannot be cross-tied and the wall fails [1]. This is the same target vancomycin uses.

Oritavancin adds two more actions: it blocks a second step in wall building and it punches through the bacterial membrane, which kills the cell faster at higher concentrations [3]. Telavancin likewise binds wall precursors, including one called lipid II, and disrupts the membrane [5].

The practical difference is how long they last. Dalbavancin has a terminal half-life (the time for blood levels to halve) of about 346 hours, roughly two weeks, which is why one infusion can cover a full course [1]. Telavancin's half-life is about 8 hours, so it is dosed once a day [5].

sections.heading: Are dalbavancin, oritavancin and telavancin FDA-approved?

blocks.text: Yes. All three are FDA-approved prescription drugs. Telavancin came first, in 2009, for complicated skin infections, and was later approved for hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia caused by Staphylococcus aureus. Dalbavancin followed in May 2014 and oritavancin in August 2014 [8]. In 2016 the FDA approved a single-infusion schedule for dalbavancin, and in 2021 it extended dalbavancin to children from birth onward [1][8]. A second oritavancin product, Kimyrsa, was approved in March 2021 with a shorter one-hour infusion [3][8].

sections.heading: What are these drugs prescribed for?

blocks.text: Their shared approval is for acute bacterial skin and skin structure infections, a category that covers cellulitis, large abscesses and infected wounds caused by susceptible Gram-positive bacteria [1][3][5]. Because a single dose of dalbavancin or oritavancin finishes treatment, they can let some patients avoid a hospital stay or a long-term IV line.

The evidence comes from large noninferiority trials, which test whether a new drug is not meaningfully worse than the standard. In the DISCOVER 1 and 2 trials of 1,312 adults, 79.7 percent on two weekly dalbavancin doses had an early response at 48 to 72 hours, against 79.8 percent on vancomycin followed by oral linezolid [6]. A later trial of 698 patients found one 1,500 mg dalbavancin infusion was not inferior to the two-dose schedule [7]. In SOLO I, a single oritavancin infusion produced an early response in 82.3 percent of patients against 78.9 percent on 7 to 10 days of twice-daily vancomycin [4]. For telavancin, the ATLAS trials in 1,867 patients reported cure in 88 percent against 87 percent on vancomycin [9].

blocks.text: Telavancin's label reserves it for pneumonia patients when alternatives are not suitable, and its kidney warnings shape when it is chosen for skin infections too [5].

For dalbavancin, the most common side effects in adults were nausea, headache and diarrhea; warnings cover serious allergic reactions, a flushing reaction if infused too fast, liver enzyme rises and Clostridioides difficile diarrhea, a gut infection that can follow any antibiotic [1]. Oritavancin's most common effects include headache, nausea, vomiting, limb abscesses and diarrhea. It also falsely prolongs some blood clotting tests for up to five days, which matters for patients on the blood thinner heparin [3].

Telavancin has the heaviest warnings. Its boxed warning, the FDA's strongest, flags higher death rates in pneumonia patients with moderate or severe kidney impairment compared with vancomycin, new or worsening kidney damage, and possible harm to a developing fetus based on limb and skeletal malformations in animal studies [5]. Taste disturbance, nausea, vomiting and foamy urine were each reported by at least 10 percent of skin infection patients [5].
